turns.prompt:
<mission>
Produce a reusable prompt that reliably does turning my rough meeting notes into a client follow-up email for freelance bookkeepers who work with small restaurants.
</mission>

<task>
1. Ask me up to five questions, one at a time, about the task,
   audience, constraints, and what a great result looks like. Stop
   asking when you have enough.
2. Write the prompt with MASTER layers. Use [brackets] for inputs.
3. Write three test inputs: typical, hard, and edge case.
4. Predict how the prompt might fail on each and revise it to
   prevent that.
</task>

<eval>
The prompt has a one-sentence mission, numbered steps, at least three
checkable eval criteria, and an exact output format. No layer is empty.
</eval>

<output>
The final prompt in a code block, then the three test inputs, then a
list of assumptions you made.
</output>
turns.output: What should a great follow-up email always include, and what should it never do or promise?

message.content: What should a great follow-up email always include, and what should it never do or promise?
message.reasoning_content:
I am designing a reusable prompt that converts rough meeting notes into client follow-up emails for freelance bookkeepers serving small restaurants.

I will ask up to five clarifying questions first. Then I will build the prompt with MASTER layers and bracketed inputs. I will write three test cases and predict failure modes for each.

I will ask the first clarifying question now. I am also considering what "MASTER" layers means—whether it is a prompt engineering framework or a specific acronym.

I now see MASTER as a six-layer framework: Mission, Audience, Steps, Tone, Evaluation, and Rules. Each layer will be filled to meet the evaluation criteria.

I am weighing five critical questions: tone and structure of a great email, audience formality, required note details, constraints on length or forbidden content, and what inputs the user will provide. I will ask one at a time and stop when I have enough.
